newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria opposition eyes victory in Sunday's poll.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria opposition eyes victory in Sunday's poll.

text.p: Reformist lawyer Petar Stoyanov looks poised to win Sunday's presidential election but Bulgaria's deep economic crisis and the shadow of political violence will leave him little time to celebrate.

As the socialist cabinet nervously braced on Friday for tough talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on sorely needed loans, opinion polls gave Stoyanov a big lead over the government's candidate, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov.
A hefty defeat for Marazov could tear apart Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's Socialist Party and derail his government's shaky economic reforms, diplomats and political analysts said.

In the Trud daily the Gallup polling agency predicted Stoyanov, candidate of the anti-communist Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), would win 64 percent of votes cast against 36 percent for Marazov in Sunday's run-off.
The Centre for Analysis and Marketing gave Stoyanov, a pro-market liberal, 57 percent and Marazov 37 percent.
"This election is very much a referendum on Videnov's record and his methods of governing," Ivan Krustev of the Centre for Liberal Strategies told Reuters.
He said a cabinet reshuffle, which Videnov firmly ruled out by this week, a new coalition government or fresh parliamentary elections were all possible scenarios if Stoyanov won.
In a televised debate on Thursday night Stoyanov accused the government of making Bulgaria the reform laggard of the former Eastern bloc and said he would call the cabinet to task if elected.
"The most important question facing us now is simply survival through the coming winter," he said.

"Bulgarians don't know what to do tomorrow - they have to choose whether to buy bread or milk or to turn on the electricity. This is a very humiliating question at the end of the 20th century," said the bespectacled Stoyanov, who is 44.

Looming bread and fuel shortages and bank closures have thrown a dark shadow over an election campaign already marred by mystery bombings and violence culminating in the October 2 assassination of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.

Lukanov, a wealthy businessman and fierce critic of the government, was gunned down as he left his Sofia home. The lack of arrests in the case has reinforced Bulgarians' belief that the police are powerless to tackle the country's crime wave.
On Wednesday a member of the Central Electoral Committee, Haralambi Anchev, narrowly escaped assassination after a home-made bomb destroyed his car.

In Thursday's debate Marazov said he would make the fight against organised crime his priority if elected but drew a sharp retort from Stoyanov that under socialist rule Bulgaria had become one of Eastern Europe's most lawless states.
Under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution the president is a largely ceremonial figure and real power lies with parliament where Videnov's socialists have a clear majority.
"But the president does have some real powers, however limited," said one diplomat, citing the head of state's right to appoint ambassadors and judges and his limited veto powers.

"(Incumbent Zhelyu) Zhelev has managed to check legislation inimical to private property and press freedoms," the diplomat said, adding that socialist domination of all institutions would be dangerous for Bulgarian democracy.
Zhelev, also a liberal, has not sought re-election after being defeated by Stoyanov in a U.S.-style primary election in June to select a single opposition presidential candidate.
The head of an IMF mission was expected to arrive in Sofia on Friday for renewed talks on unblocking loans desperately needed to help Bulgaria meet heavy debt repayments.
Anxious to avoid default on its $10 billion of foreign debt, the government has offered for privatisation some 20 big state firms that it hopes will raise around $1 billion.
